script.opening: (Mother, worried, speaks first.) "Her fingers go completely dead white in the cold — then blue — and they really hurt when they warm up. My friend said it might be poor circulation, or is it something to do with her heart? She's 15, I just want to know it's nothing serious." (Ruby, quietly) "It's annoying at school — PE outside is the worst."

facts.text: (Ruby) "They go white, like dead, then blue. And when they warm up they go red and really hurt." Numb and tingly while white. Last 10–20 minutes. Two winters now. Triggered by cold, sometimes by holding a cold drink. (Ruby) "Both hands. Mostly the same fingers each side." Toes sometimes too.
(Ruby) "They go back to normal. No sores." No pits or ulcers on the fingertips, no tight or shiny skin, no swollen fingers. Will show her hands and fingertips on camera.

(Ruby) "No, none of that" — no joint pains or swelling, no rashes (including on the face in sun), no mouth ulcers, no dry eyes or mouth, no trouble swallowing, no hair loss, no breathlessness, no fevers or weight loss, no tiredness beyond normal.
(Mother) "No, nothing." No regular medicines, no contraceptive pill, no ADHD medicines, no migraine treatment. Healthy, no heart problems. No allergies.
If asked: Mum's sister "has cold hands". No lupus, scleroderma or rheumatoid arthritis in the family that they know of.
Year 10 student. Doesn't smoke or vape (if asked alone: "No, honestly"). Mum's partner smokes outside. Drinks two energy drinks a day sometimes. Plays netball.
Happy to talk alone for a minute if offered. Nothing to disclose — no smoking, not sexually active, mood fine. Feels a bit embarrassed that teachers think she is making a fuss.

Mum is anxious and does most of the talking; Ruby is shy but answers clearly if asked directly. If the doctor only talks to Mum, Ruby goes silent. (Mother) "That it's a sign of something serious. You read things online. She's only 15." (Ruby) "It's just annoying. I don't like making a fuss." Mum is reassured by a clear explanation and asks for a letter for school.

ice.ideas: (Mother) "Poor circulation — or something with her heart." (Ruby) "Just cold hands."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — (Mother) she has read online that it can be a sign of a serious disease and is frightened. (Ruby) PE in winter is painful and embarrassing; she doesn't want to make a fuss.
ice.expectations: (Mother) To be told it's nothing serious. (Ruby) Something practical for school — like being allowed gloves in PE.

cues: (Mother) "Is it something to do with her heart?" — the worry to address directly.
(Ruby) "PE outside is the worst." — the practical impact; invites talking to Ruby.
(Ruby) "I don't like making a fuss." — may under-report; check directly.

checkpoints.text: Recognises RAYNAUD’S PHENOMENON from the triphasic colour change (white→blue→red), cold/stress trigger, numbness/pain and full inter-attack recovery

Performs the KEY primary-vs-secondary distinction — actively screening for secondary red flags (later onset, asymmetry, digital ulcers/pits/gangrene, abnormal nailfold capillaries) and associated CTD features (arthralgia, skin tightening, rash, sicca symptoms, dysphagia, mouth ulcers, fatigue)

Recognises the reassuring PRIMARY picture in Ruby (teenage female, symmetrical, no tissue damage, no systemic features) and examines appropriately (digits, nailfold capillaries, pulses, BP) — arranging this face to face because it cannot be done properly on video

Orders proportionate investigations (FBC, ESR/CRP, ANA ± ENA) to support the diagnosis/catch early CTD, and refers to (paediatric/adolescent) rheumatology if any secondary feature or positive autoantibodies

Advises conservative management of primary Raynaud’s (keep warm/gloves/hand warmers, avoid sudden cold, no smoking incl. household, limit caffeine, avoid precipitant drugs) and knows nifedipine is the usual first drug if severe but is off-label under 18 (adult-only licence) and started only with specialist advice, dose per BNFC
Engages RUBY directly about the impact (school, PE, self-image) and supports her understanding, involving the mother without talking over the patient, and offering her time on her own

Addresses the mother’s "is it her heart/something serious?" honestly and proportionately — reassuring about benign primary Raynaud’s while explaining the checks for the small chance of an underlying cause

Safety-nets and follows up: what change would warrant review (ulcers/sores on fingertips, asymmetry, new joint/skin/systemic symptoms), with a same-day call for a finger that stays white or blue and will not rewarm (critical digital ischaemia), the plan for any bloods/referral, practical school advice, and review — proportionate care, neither over-investigating nor missing secondary disease

worked.txt: (To Ruby first.) "What you’re describing — fingers going white, then blue, then red and sore in the cold — has a name: Raynaud’s. It’s the small blood vessels in your fingers over-reacting to cold. It’s really common, especially in younger women." (To mum) "It’s not the heart."

"There are two kinds, and my main job today is to check which. Ruby — do you ever get sores or ulcers on your fingertips? Any joint pains, rashes, dry eyes or mouth, trouble swallowing, mouth ulcers, or feeling really tired? … None of that. Good — that’s reassuring."

"Could you hold your hands up to the camera? … No sores or scars that I can see. I can’t check the little vessels at your nails, your pulses or blood pressure properly on video, so I’d like to see you in person for that. So far it all points to the common, harmless type — it doesn’t damage your fingers. I’ll do a couple of blood tests at the same visit just to be thorough."

"The biggest helpers are practical: keep your whole self warm, not just hands — gloves, layers, hand warmers in your coat for PE. Avoid going from warm to freezing suddenly. Easy on the energy drinks and coffee, and definitely no smoking or vaping, which makes it worse."

"If it ever gets bad enough to really interfere — lots of painful attacks — there’s a tablet called nifedipine that relaxes those vessels. It’s licensed for adults, so for someone your age we’d only use it with advice from a specialist. We don’t need it now, but it’s there if things step up."

"If a finger ever stays white or blue and won’t warm up, call us the same day. Come back if Ruby gets any sores or ulcers on her fingertips, if one hand’s much worse than the other, or if any of those other things appear — joint pains, rashes, swallowing trouble. Otherwise this is very manageable. Ruby, anything you wanted to ask me yourself? And if you ever want to talk to me on your own about anything, that’s always fine."

f.learning: The triphasic digital colour change — WHITE (vasospasm) → BLUE (cyanosis) → RED (reperfusion) — on cold/stress exposure, with numbness/pain and full recovery between attacks, is RAYNAUD’S PHENOMENON, and the key examinable skill is distinguishing PRIMARY from SECONDARY disease. PRIMARY (idiopathic) Raynaud’s is common and benign: onset in the teens/twenties, typically female, symmetrical, with no tissue damage (no digital ulcers/pits/gangrene), normal nailfold capillaries, no systemic features, and negative autoantibodies/normal inflammatory markers. SECONDARY Raynaud’s points to an underlying connective tissue disease (systemic sclerosis/scleroderma, SLE, mixed CTD) and is flagged by later onset (>30–40), asymmetry, severe attacks, digital ulcers/pitting scars/gangrene, abnormal nailfold capillaries, and associated features (arthralgia, skin tightening/puffiness, malar or photosensitive rash, dry eyes/mouth, dysphagia/reflux, mouth ulcers, hair loss, fatigue) — so screen these actively. Investigations are proportionate: examine hands, nailfolds, pulses and BP face to face (not possible on video); a purely primary picture with normal examination needs little, though FBC, ESR/CRP and ANA (± ENA) reasonably support the diagnosis and catch early CTD; any secondary red flag or positive autoantibodies warrants these bloods and rheumatology referral. Manage primary Raynaud’s conservatively first — keep the whole body warm (gloves, hand warmers, layers, avoid sudden cold), stop smoking (including household exposure), limit caffeine and avoid precipitant drugs — with nifedipine the usual first drug if attacks are frequent/severe (licensed for adults only, so off-label and specialist-advised under 18, dose per BNFC), reassuring that primary Raynaud’s does not damage the fingers while safety-netting for same-day assessment of a digit that will not rewarm or new ulceration/necrosis (BSR 2024). Engage the teenager directly about real-life impact (school, PE, self-image), offer her time on her own, and reassure the anxious parent proportionately.

knowledge.guideline: BSR guideline for the management of systemic sclerosis (2024) · EULAR systemic sclerosis recommendations (2023 update, international) · PCDS Raynaud’s phenomenon · GMC 0–18 years (2018)
knowledge.summary: Symmetrical white–blue–red colour change in the cold in a well 15-year-old is almost always primary Raynaud’s. The skill is a careful screen for secondary features, warmth-first management, and speaking to Ruby herself.

points.t: Episodic colour change of the digits on cold or stress — white, then blue, then red on rewarming — with numbness or pain and full recovery between attacks.
Onset in the teens or twenties, symmetrical, no ulcers or pitting scars, normal nailfolds, no systemic features. It does not damage the fingers.

Later onset, asymmetry, digital ulcers, pitting scars or necrosis, abnormal nailfold capillaries, skin tightening or puffy fingers, rash, joint pain, mouth ulcers, dry eyes or mouth, swallowing problems, fatigue. These point to connective tissue disease, most often systemic sclerosis (BSR 2024).

Examine hands, nailfolds (a dermatoscope helps), pulses and BP face to face. Typical primary Raynaud’s is a clinical diagnosis: no routine bloods or ANA (PCDS), because a positive ANA is often non-specific. If any secondary feature is found, check FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, urinalysis and ANA (ENA and further tests guided by findings) and refer to paediatric or adolescent rheumatology.

Keep the whole body warm, gloves and hand warmers, avoid sudden cold, rewarm gently with warm not hot water, avoid smoking and vaping, and review triggering medicines such as decongestants. A school plan helps with PE outdoors.

Nifedipine is the only medicine licensed for Raynaud’s in the UK, for adults; in under-18s it is off-label and best started with specialist advice (dose per BNFC). A digit that stays white or blue, new ulceration or necrosis → same-day assessment (BSR 2024: preferably within 48 hours for new necrosis).

dg.d: Greeted both; took the history from Ruby in her own words; let her mother add.
Explored school and PE, how she feels about it around others, and the mother’s worry.
Face-to-face hands, nailfolds, pulses and BP. No routine bloods if typical; FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, urinalysis and ANA only if secondary features.
Primary vs secondary Raynaud’s; systemic sclerosis, SLE, mixed connective tissue disease; drug triggers.
Asked about asymmetry, ulcers, pitting and connective tissue features; knows a non-reperfusing digit or new necrosis needs same-day assessment.
Named primary Raynaud’s as most likely, while explaining the checks.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Warmth-first plan chosen with Ruby; school letter; nifedipine only with specialist advice in under-18s (off-label; dose per BNFC).
Advice on smoking and vaping, decongestants and other triggers; plan for bloods and rheumatology if any secondary feature.
Named ulcers, a digit that won’t warm, and new systemic symptoms; results review booked; teach-back from Ruby.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up ‘PE outside is the worst’ and ‘is it her heart’; acted on each.
Mother’s idea: poor circulation or the heart; concern: serious disease. Ruby’s concern: pain and nuisance at school. Expectation: reassurance.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — (Mother) she has read online that it can be a sign of a serious disease and is frightened. (Ruby) PE in winter is painful and embarrassing; she doesn't want to make a fuss — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Lee. Ruby, thanks for coming — and hello to Mum. Ruby, you said PE outside is the worst. Can you tell me what happens to your fingers?
model.why: Greets both, then turns to Ruby and picks up her own words

model.text: (Ruby) “They go white, like dead, then blue. And when they warm up they go red and really hurt.”

Thank you, that’s a really clear description. I’d like to ask you a few questions, have a look at your hands on the camera, and then explain what I think it is and what we can do. Mum, I’ll come to your questions too — is that okay with you both?
model.why: Agenda that includes both and keeps Ruby central

model.text: (Mother) “Of course.” (Ruby nods.)
Ruby, is it both hands, and all the fingers, or just one or two? And does it ever affect your toes?
model.why: Checks symmetry — a key primary vs secondary feature

model.text: (Ruby) “Both hands. Mostly the same fingers each side.”
Once your hands warm up, do they go completely back to normal? Have you ever had sores or little cuts on your fingertips that were slow to heal?
model.why: Screens for tissue damage — digital ulcers and pitting

model.text: (Ruby) “They go back to normal. No sores.”

I’m going to ask about a few other things that might sound unrelated. Any painful or swollen joints, rashes — especially on your face in the sun — mouth ulcers, dry or gritty eyes, trouble swallowing, your skin feeling tight on your fingers, or being really tired?
model.why: Targeted screen for connective tissue disease

model.text: (Ruby) “No, none of that.”
Are you taking anything — tablets, cold remedies, anything from the chemist?
(Mother) “No, nothing.”
Could you hold your hands up to the camera, fingertips first? … They look a normal colour now, with no sores or scars I can see.
model.why: Video look at the hands, acknowledging its limits

model.text: Mum, you mentioned poor circulation, or her heart. What’s been worrying you most?
model.why: Explores the parent’s idea and concern directly

model.text: (Mother) “That it’s a sign of something serious. You read things online. She’s only 15.”
That’s a completely understandable worry. And Ruby, how is it affecting you day to day?
model.why: Validates the mother, then returns to Ruby’s experience

model.text: (Ruby) “PE in winter is horrible. My fingers hurt and I can’t do anything.”
That sounds really frustrating. How do you feel about it at school, with other people around?
model.why: Acknowledges and explores the teenager’s experience

model.text: (Ruby) “It’s just annoying. I don’t like making a fuss.”
Ruby, this is called Raynaud’s. The tiny blood vessels in your fingers overreact to cold and squeeze shut for a while, which is why they go white, then blue, then red when the blood rushes back.

Mum, it isn’t a heart problem. At Ruby’s age, both hands, no sores, and nothing else going on, this is almost always the common, harmless type. It doesn’t damage the fingers. Very occasionally it’s linked to a condition affecting the immune system, which is why I asked all those other questions.
model.why: Proportionate reassurance with the reason for the secondary screen

model.text: (Mother) “So you don’t think it’s anything bad?”

Everything so far points to the harmless type. To be thorough, I’d like to see Ruby in person to check her fingers, nail beds, pulses and blood pressure, If everything looks normal, she won’t need blood tests. If I find anything unusual, I’d do some blood tests and ask the young people’s rheumatology team to see her.
model.why: Face-to-face examination, bloods only if secondary features, and a clear referral trigger

model.text: Ruby, the main treatment is keeping your whole body warm, not just your hands. Good gloves, hand warmers, layers, and warming up gently with warm — not hot — water. Smoking and vaping make it worse too. Which of those could you actually do at school?
model.why: Warmth-first advice, involving Ruby in choices

model.text: (Ruby) “Gloves in PE, if they let me. And hand warmers in my bag.”

Good plan. I can write a short letter for school so you can wear gloves and warm up indoors when it’s cold. There are medicines for severe cases, but for someone your age we’d only use one with specialist advice, and you may not need it.
model.why: School adjustment and proportionate view of nifedipine

model.text: (Mother) “A letter would be really helpful.”

Please get in touch if Ruby gets sores on her fingertips, if one finger stays white or blue and won’t warm up — that’s a same-day call — or if she develops joint pains, rashes, tight skin or swallowing problems. Ruby, can you tell me what you’ll do next time it happens?
model.why: Specific safety-net and teach-back to the patient

model.text: (Ruby) “Get somewhere warm, warm my hands slowly, and tell Mum if a finger doesn’t come back.”
Perfect. I’ll book the appointment for the hands check, and we’ll go through what I find together. Ruby, if you ever want to talk to me on your own about anything, that’s always fine.
model.why: Closes with follow-up and offers the teenager her own space

social.t: Outdoor PE and cold classrooms trigger attacks; not wanting to make a fuss. A short plan with school helps.
At 15, Ruby should lead the conversation. Offer time alone to discuss anything she prefers not to say in front of her mother.

legal.t: GMC 0–18 years guidance (2018): a young person who understands the decision can consent to their own care, and their confidentiality is respected unless there is a risk of serious harm.

Children and Families Act 2014 (section 100) and DfE statutory guidance ‘Supporting pupils at school with medical conditions’: schools should make arrangements, such as gloves in PE, for pupils with medical conditions.

professional.t: Nifedipine is licensed for Raynaud’s in adults only. Off-label use in a child needs a clear rationale and informed consent, ideally with specialist advice (GMC good practice in prescribing, 2021).

community.t: Scleroderma and Raynaud’s UK (SRUK) for information for young people and families, including practical tips for school.

redFlags: Digit that stays white or blue and does not reperfuse, new ulceration or necrosis → same-day assessment
Asymmetry, single-digit involvement, digital ulcers or pitting scars → suggests secondary Raynaud’s
Skin tightening, puffy fingers, rash, joint pain, mouth ulcers, sicca symptoms, dysphagia, fatigue → bloods and rheumatology
psychosocial: Pain and nuisance at school, especially outdoor PE
Ruby’s own understanding and what she can manage at school
ice: Idea (mother): poor circulation, or something to do with the heart
Concern: a serious underlying disease at 15; Ruby — pain at school, especially PE
Expectation: to be told it’s nothing serious

playbook.diagnosis: “This is Raynaud’s — the small blood vessels in the fingers overreact to cold. At Ruby’s age, with both hands affected and no sores or other symptoms, it’s almost always the harmless type.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the blood vessels in your fingers as taps that turn off too hard in the cold. When they turn back on, the blood rushes in — that’s the red and the pain. The taps themselves aren’t damaged.”

management.reflectIce: “Mum, you asked if it’s her heart — it isn’t. And Ruby, you said PE is the worst, so let’s make a plan for that.”
management.psychosocial: Let Ruby choose the practical measures she will use; offer a school letter; offer her time alone.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face check: hands, nailfolds, pulses, BP; bloods (FBC, ESR or CRP, ANA) only if secondary features
Warmth-first: whole-body warmth, gloves, hand warmers, gentle rewarming; avoid smoking, vaping and decongestants
School letter; bloods and rheumatology if secondary features; nifedipine only with specialist advice if severe
safetyNet: Fingertip sores or a finger that won’t warm up → same-day contact
New joint pain, rash, tight skin or swallowing problems → review; results discussed together

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by talking to the wrong person or by stopping at the label. The patterns below come up repeatedly.

items.fail: Taking the whole history from the mother.
items.why: A 15-year-old is the patient; Relating to Others marks depend on engaging her.
items.fix: Start with Ruby’s words and keep turning back to her.

items.why: The task is the primary vs secondary distinction. Missing connective tissue features delays diagnosis.
items.fix: Ask about symmetry, ulcers, pitting and systemic features every time.

items.fail: Starting nifedipine at the first consultation.
items.why: Warmth-first is enough for most; nifedipine is off-label in under-18s and needs a clear reason.
items.fix: Lifestyle and school measures first; specialist advice if attacks remain severe.

items.why: An unaddressed parental fear undermines the whole plan.
items.fix: Answer it directly: “It isn’t a heart problem.”

items.why: A digit that doesn’t reperfuse or new ulceration needs same-day assessment.
items.fix: Name it plainly: “If a finger stays white or blue and won’t warm up, call us the same day.”

items.fail: Over-investigating and alarming: naming lupus and scleroderma up front.
items.why: Disproportionate worry and language not pitched to a teenager.
items.fix: Explain the small chance simply, and the simple checks you’ll do.

SCA_MODELS.text: Ruby, the main treatment is keeping your whole body warm, not just your hands. Good gloves, hand warmers, layers, and warming up gently with warm — not hot — water. Smoking and vaping make it worse too. Which of those could you actually do at school?
SCA_MODELS.why: Warmth-first advice, involving Ruby in choices

SCA_MODELS.text: (Ruby) “Gloves in PE, if they let me. And hand warmers in my bag.”

Good plan. I can write a short letter for school so you can wear gloves and warm up indoors when it’s cold. There are medicines for severe cases, but for someone your age we’d only use one with specialist advice, and you may not need it.
SCA_MODELS.why: School adjustment and proportionate view of nifedipine

SCA_MODELS.text: (Mother) “A letter would be really helpful.”

Please get in touch if Ruby gets sores on her fingertips, if one finger stays white or blue and won’t warm up — that’s a same-day call — or if she develops joint pains, rashes, tight skin or swallowing problems. Ruby, can you tell me what you’ll do next time it happens?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and teach-back to the patient

SCA_MODELS.text: (Ruby) “Get somewhere warm, warm my hands slowly, and tell Mum if a finger doesn’t come back.”
Perfect. I’ll book the appointment for the hands check, and we’ll go through what I find together. Ruby, if you ever want to talk to me on your own about anything, that’s always fine.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with follow-up and offers the teenager her own space

SCA_STEM.name: Ruby Hartnell
SCA_STEM.recent: Mother reports two winters of fingers turning white, then blue, then red in the cold, with numbness, tingling and pain on rewarming, fully settling between attacks. Otherwise well.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation with her mother: “Is it just poor circulation?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BSR guideline for the management of systemic sclerosis (2024) · EULAR systemic sclerosis recommendations (2023 update, international) · PCDS Raynaud’s phenomenon · GMC 0–18 years (2018)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Symmetrical white–blue–red colour change in the cold in a well 15-year-old is almost always primary Raynaud’s. The skill is a careful screen for secondary features, warmth-first management, and speaking to Ruby herself.

points.t: Episodic colour change of the digits on cold or stress — white, then blue, then red on rewarming — with numbness or pain and full recovery between attacks.
Onset in the teens or twenties, symmetrical, no ulcers or pitting scars, normal nailfolds, no systemic features. It does not damage the fingers.

Later onset, asymmetry, digital ulcers, pitting scars or necrosis, abnormal nailfold capillaries, skin tightening or puffy fingers, rash, joint pain, mouth ulcers, dry eyes or mouth, swallowing problems, fatigue. These point to connective tissue disease, most often systemic sclerosis (BSR 2024).

Examine hands, nailfolds (a dermatoscope helps), pulses and BP face to face. Typical primary Raynaud’s is a clinical diagnosis: no routine bloods or ANA (PCDS), because a positive ANA is often non-specific. If any secondary feature is found, check FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, urinalysis and ANA (ENA and further tests guided by findings) and refer to paediatric or adolescent rheumatology.

Keep the whole body warm, gloves and hand warmers, avoid sudden cold, rewarm gently with warm not hot water, avoid smoking and vaping, and review triggering medicines such as decongestants. A school plan helps with PE outdoors.

Nifedipine is the only medicine licensed for Raynaud’s in the UK, for adults; in under-18s it is off-label and best started with specialist advice (dose per BNFC). A digit that stays white or blue, new ulceration or necrosis → same-day assessment (BSR 2024: preferably within 48 hours for new necrosis).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Greeted both; took the history from Ruby in her own words; let her mother add.
Explored school and PE, how she feels about it around others, and the mother’s worry.
Picked up ‘PE outside is the worst’ and ‘is it her heart’; acted on each.
Mother’s idea: poor circulation or the heart; concern: serious disease. Ruby’s concern: pain and nuisance at school. Expectation: reassurance.
Face-to-face hands, nailfolds, pulses and BP. No routine bloods if typical; FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, urinalysis and ANA only if secondary features.
Primary vs secondary Raynaud’s; systemic sclerosis, SLE, mixed connective tissue disease; drug triggers.
Asked about asymmetry, ulcers, pitting and connective tissue features; knows a non-reperfusing digit or new necrosis needs same-day assessment.
Named primary Raynaud’s as most likely, while explaining the checks.
Warmth-first plan chosen with Ruby; school letter; nifedipine only with specialist advice in under-18s (off-label; dose per BNFC).
Advice on smoking and vaping, decongestants and other triggers; plan for bloods and rheumatology if any secondary feature.
Named ulcers, a digit that won’t warm, and new systemic symptoms; results review booked; teach-back from Ruby.

social.t: Outdoor PE and cold classrooms trigger attacks; not wanting to make a fuss. A short plan with school helps.
At 15, Ruby should lead the conversation. Offer time alone to discuss anything she prefers not to say in front of her mother.

legal.t: GMC 0–18 years guidance (2018): a young person who understands the decision can consent to their own care, and their confidentiality is respected unless there is a risk of serious harm.

Children and Families Act 2014 (section 100) and DfE statutory guidance ‘Supporting pupils at school with medical conditions’: schools should make arrangements, such as gloves in PE, for pupils with medical conditions.

professional.t: Nifedipine is licensed for Raynaud’s in adults only. Off-label use in a child needs a clear rationale and informed consent, ideally with specialist advice (GMC good practice in prescribing, 2021).

community.t: Scleroderma and Raynaud’s UK (SRUK) for information for young people and families, including practical tips for school.

redFlags: Digit that stays white or blue and does not reperfuse, new ulceration or necrosis → same-day assessment
Asymmetry, single-digit involvement, digital ulcers or pitting scars → suggests secondary Raynaud’s
Skin tightening, puffy fingers, rash, joint pain, mouth ulcers, sicca symptoms, dysphagia, fatigue → bloods and rheumatology
psychosocial: Pain and nuisance at school, especially outdoor PE
Ruby’s own understanding and what she can manage at school
ice: Idea (mother): poor circulation, or something to do with the heart
Concern: a serious underlying disease at 15; Ruby — pain at school, especially PE
Expectation: to be told it’s nothing serious

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is Raynaud’s — the small blood vessels in the fingers overreact to cold. At Ruby’s age, with both hands affected and no sores or other symptoms, it’s almost always the harmless type.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the blood vessels in your fingers as taps that turn off too hard in the cold. When they turn back on, the blood rushes in — that’s the red and the pain. The taps themselves aren’t damaged.”

management.reflectIce: “Mum, you asked if it’s her heart — it isn’t. And Ruby, you said PE is the worst, so let’s make a plan for that.”
management.psychosocial: Let Ruby choose the practical measures she will use; offer a school letter; offer her time alone.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face check: hands, nailfolds, pulses, BP; bloods (FBC, ESR or CRP, ANA) only if secondary features
Warmth-first: whole-body warmth, gloves, hand warmers, gentle rewarming; avoid smoking, vaping and decongestants
School letter; bloods and rheumatology if secondary features; nifedipine only with specialist advice if severe
safetyNet: Fingertip sores or a finger that won’t warm up → same-day contact
New joint pain, rash, tight skin or swallowing problems → review; results discussed together

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by talking to the wrong person or by stopping at the label. The patterns below come up repeatedly.

items.fail: Taking the whole history from the mother.
items.why: A 15-year-old is the patient; Relating to Others marks depend on engaging her.
items.fix: Start with Ruby’s words and keep turning back to her.

items.why: The task is the primary vs secondary distinction. Missing connective tissue features delays diagnosis.
items.fix: Ask about symmetry, ulcers, pitting and systemic features every time.

items.fail: Starting nifedipine at the first consultation.
items.why: Warmth-first is enough for most; nifedipine is off-label in under-18s and needs a clear reason.
items.fix: Lifestyle and school measures first; specialist advice if attacks remain severe.

items.why: An unaddressed parental fear undermines the whole plan.
items.fix: Answer it directly: “It isn’t a heart problem.”

items.why: A digit that doesn’t reperfuse or new ulceration needs same-day assessment.
items.fix: Name it plainly: “If a finger stays white or blue and won’t warm up, call us the same day.”

items.fail: Over-investigating and alarming: naming lupus and scleroderma up front.
items.why: Disproportionate worry and language not pitched to a teenager.
items.fix: Explain the small chance simply, and the simple checks you’ll do.
